paragraphs: When the earthquake of 1929 off the Grand Banks of Newfoundland severed a dozen transatlantic telegraph cables, the damage was at first blamed on the shaking itself. Only in 1952 did two geologists notice what the repair logs had recorded all along: the cables nearest the epicenter had parted at the moment of the shock, but those farther down the continental slope had failed one after another over the following thirteen hours, in strict order of distance. A flow of sediment-laden water, they argued, had poured down the slope like an avalanche, and from the timing of the breaks they computed its speed. The ramifications reached well beyond the cables. The turbidity current, until then a laboratory curiosity, became the favored explanation for much that had puzzled students of the deep seafloor, from beds of graded sand lying hundreds of kilometers from any shore to the canyons notched into the continental margins.

The cable evidence has worn better than some of what was built on it. The sequence of breaks is hard to explain any other way, and the evidence adduced since, including cables cut in order down the slopes off Taiwan in 2006, has only confirmed it. What the cables cannot reveal is how typical the 1929 flow was. Because the logs record only the moments at which cables parted, the speeds computed from them describe the current's leading edge, the fastest part of a flow whose body may have moved far more slowly; and a reading drawn from a single catastrophic event says nothing about whether the canyons were cut by rare flows of that size or by many smaller ones that no cable would have registered. To treat the Grand Banks flow as the archetypal turbidity current, as textbooks long did, is to assume that the one flow that happened to be measured is the kind that does most of the work.

The great Russian novels of the 1860s and 1870s reached their first readers not as books but in monthly installments of the “thick journals,” periodicals whose ambit ran from agronomy and statistics to the reform of the courts. Critics who fault these novels for their wayward digressions, the chapters on threshing machines or ecclesiastical law that seem to halt the story, have usually read them in bound editions, where such chapters interrupt scenes of mounting suspense. In the journals they kept different company: a subscriber who turned from an article on provincial budgets to the month's installment found the novel's essayistic chapters continuous with the pages around them, and editors expected a novelist to address the same questions as the economists who preceded him. None of this makes every digression a success; some were plainly padding, written to fill out an installment when the novelist had fallen behind with his plot, and payment by the printed sheet left him little recourse but to pad. It does suggest, however, that the standard of unity by which the novels have so often been found wanting was one their first readers had little reason to apply, and that to judge them by it alone is reductive.

Ecologists studying the Brannock Range attribute the recovery of streamside willows there since wolves were reintroduced not to any reduction in elk numbers, which have held steady, but to elk avoiding places where wolves can ambush them, chiefly stream banks screened by dense brush. Along the streams of the range's eastern valleys, however, where the banks are just as brushy and wolves just as numerous as elsewhere in the range, the willows have shown no recovery at all.

In the standard history of scurvy, the decisive moment comes in 1747, when James Lind, a surgeon aboard a British warship, divided twelve stricken sailors into pairs, gave each pair a different remedy, and found that the two who received oranges and lemons recovered within days. The story has the shape of a parable: a lone visionary, a controlled comparison, an unambiguous result, and then a scandalous delay of nearly half a century before the Admiralty issued lemon juice to the fleet. Historians who tell it this way treat the delay as institutional inertia, the failure of a hidebound navy to act on what one of its own surgeons had shown.

A revisionist account, now dominant among historians of medicine, begins with Lind's own treatise and finds in it scarcely a scintilla of the parable. Lind described the trial in a few paragraphs of a book running to several hundred pages, and he did not conclude from it that scurvy was a disease of deficiency. He held, with most physicians of his day, that it arose when damp sea air clogged the pores, and he valued citrus as one of several agents that might restore perspiration; he even recommended a boiled concentrate of lemon juice whose preparation, it is now known, destroyed most of the vitamin it contained. On this reading the delay was not inertia at all: no one, Lind included, had reason to regard the trial as decisive, and the navy's eventual adoption of lemon juice owed more to the advocacy of a later physician, Gilbert Blane, than to anything Lind had shown.

The revisionists are right about Lind's theory, and right that the trial meant less to him than it does to us. But their account often slides from the claim that Lind misunderstood his result to the claim that the result was unavailable to his contemporaries, and the second does not follow from the first. Naval surgeons did not need a theory of vitamins to notice that crews supplied with fresh citrus stayed well, and several recorded as much in their journals before Blane had written a word on the subject. What they lacked was not evidence but any means of making evidence surmount the authority of a received theory, and that lack, unlike Lind's error, belongs to the institution rather than to the man. The older story misplaced the scandal; it did not invent it.

Archaeologists call an object a skeuomorph when it reproduces, in a new material, a feature that was functional only in the old one: the clay cup with molded “rivets” copied from a hammered bronze original, or the stone ax whose ridged butt imitates the casting seam of a metal one. The term, coined by a Victorian antiquarian, is often used as if it explained something, but it merely names a pattern, and at least two quite different processes produce it. In the first, the copy is a cheap substitute for a prized original, and the useless feature is kept precisely because it advertises the costlier material; potters who could not afford bronze were, on this view, borrowing its prestige, and a grave assemblage full of such cups records an aspiration as much as a poverty. In the second, the feature survives because no one thought to drop it: craftspeople reproducing a familiar form carry its details over by habit, as atavistic traces of the form's history, much as the builders of the first iron bridges joined their castings with the dovetails and wedges of carpentry. The two processes can be told apart, at least in principle. Emulation should be most faithful where the original was most admired and should lapse once the original ceases to be rare, whereas habit should erode slowly and with no regard to the standing of the model.

European readers who met the Persian ghazal in translation in the late eighteenth century tended to admire its couplets one at a time and to despair of the poem as a whole; the line “like orient pearls at random strung,” which an English translator of Hafez put into the poet's own mouth, became a catchword for a form supposed to have no principle of order beyond its rhyme. The charge rested partly on a misreading of convention. Each couplet of a ghazal was expected to be complete in itself, and a reader steeped in the tradition took pleasure in watching a stock image, the moth and the candle or the nightingale and the rose, refract into a new meaning within two lines, its valence shifting from the erotic to the allegorical and back; to demand of such a poem the sustained argument of an ode is to fault it for declining an undertaking it never made. Yet the defense can be pressed too far. Persian commentators ranked ghazals partly by the subtlety of the threads that ran between their couplets, and the compilers of manuscript anthologies sometimes reordered a poem's couplets, a liberty that suggests they found its sequence meaningful enough to improve, though a skeptic might take it as proof that they found the sequence negotiable.

Last year the Ashby school district moved recess at its elementary schools from after lunch to before it. Over the following school year, the weight of food that students threw away from their lunch trays fell by a third. District officials conclude that children who play before they eat come to lunch hungrier and so finish more of their meals.

questions.prompt: Admirers of the dyers' guild have long cited its support for the city's first sewer ordinance as proof of its civic spirit, but the minute books tell a less flattering story: the guild opposed the ordinance through three readings and came round only in the week its own members were named contractors for the digging, a sequence that makes its conversion look less public-minded than ___.

explanation.key: The “but” sets the minute books against the civic-spirit reading, and the sequence they record (opposed through three readings, converted the week its members got the digging contracts) points to gain. “Less public-minded than ___” asks for the motive the sequence suggests instead: mercenary, moved by profit.

distractors.altruistic: Means public-minded; reading “less … than” backwards gives the admirers' view.
distractors.inadvertent: The timing is the evidence, not an accident, and an accident is not a motive set against public-mindedness.
distractors.rancorous: Nothing suggests a grudge; the clue is the contract, not bitterness.
distractors.callous: Indifference to suffering is a different fault; the evidence is about gain.

questions.prompt: The curators hoped that a case of medieval surgical instruments, each finer than the tools of most modern hobbyists, would (i) ___ visitors of the belief that early surgeons were little better than butchers. The comment books suggest the display did more than that: many visitors wrote that it had (ii) ___ in them an interest in the history of medicine they had never expected to feel.

explanation.key: (i) Instruments finer than modern tools contradict the butcher stereotype, so the curators wanted to free visitors of it: disabuse. (ii) “Did more than that” and an interest “they had never expected to feel” mean the display aroused one: kindled, in its sense of stirring a feeling, not lighting a fire.

distractors.apprise: To inform someone of something; the curators meant to correct the belief, not report it.
distractors.persuade: “Persuade visitors of the belief” would confirm the stereotype the instruments contradict.
distractors.allayed: One allays a fear or a doubt, not a new interest.
distractors.feigned: The visitors, not the display, could feign an interest, and their notes say it was real.

questions.prompt: The sanitary committee's early pamphlets were unabashedly (i) ___, crowded with capital letters, verses of scripture and the names of children lost to the summer fevers. Its later pamphlets read as flat inventories of drains and cisterns, and historians have taken the change of tone for a loss of nerve. It was nearer the reverse: an authority that had remained (ii) ___ for as long as the vestry, without opposing the committee's rules, merely (iii) ___ them became a real one once the vestry began to fine householders who broke them, and a body whose rules carry fines has no further need to plead.

explanation.key: (i) Undecidable from the first sentence alone; the last clause settles it: a body with fines “has no further need to plead,” so the early pamphlets pleaded and urged: hortatory. (ii) Set against “became a real one”: nominal, existing in name only. (iii) “Without opposing … merely” describes passive acceptance without enforcement: acquiesced in.

distractors.pithy: “Crowded with” capitals, scripture and names runs against concision, and the contrast drawn is pleading versus flat inventory.
distractors.discursive: Rambling fits “crowded,” but the passage's turn is from pleading to stating, not from digressive to focused.
distractors.tacit: Unspoken, not the opposite of real.
distractors.manifest: The reverse of the sense needed: the authority was not yet real.
distractors.insisted on: A vestry insisting on the rules would already have given them force, so the authority would not have stayed nominal; it also clashes with “merely.”

questions.prompt: Those who still cite the hoard as proof that the harbor town was sacked in a single raid must reckon with the coins themselves: struck over some sixty years and worn to every degree from mint-fresh to nearly smooth, they ___ the story of one panicked burial and suggest instead a household's savings, added to across generations.

explanation.key: Coins struck over sixty years and worn to every degree cannot have gone into the ground in one panic, and “suggest instead” marks a contradiction: the coins prove the single-raid story false. Refute and debunk.

distractors.corroborate: Trap pair with substantiate: true synonyms, but “must reckon with” and “suggest instead” call for the opposite polarity.
distractors.embellish: To add detail to a picture, not to overturn it.
distractors.implicate: To involve someone in wrongdoing; it does not take “the picture” as its object in this sense.

questions.prompt: Within a year of the bridge's opening, the same newspapers that had ___ it as the engineering marvel of the age were printing letters from carters who refused to cross it on windy days, when its deck swayed visibly under the lightest load.

explanation.key: “The same newspapers that had ___ it” sets their earlier verdict against the complaints they now print, a reversal over time; the pointed “same” only makes sense if they had once praised it as a marvel: extol and hail (“hail it as” = acclaim it as).

distractors.denounce: Trap pair with decry: papers that had condemned the bridge printing complaints would be no reversal, and “the same” would be pointless.
distractors.impute: To attribute a quality or fault; it does not take “it as the engineering marvel.”

questions.prompt: Because the serum could be given only after the bite, its makers never pretended that it could prevent infection; the trial asked instead whether, in patients already infected, it could ___ the disease, shortening the fever and sparing the nerves the damage that had left earlier survivors lame.

explanation.key: The serum works on patients already infected, and its hoped-for effect is spelled out after the comma: a shorter fever and less damage. It lessens the disease's severity: mitigate and attenuate.

distractors.avert: To stop from happening; the disease is already under way in these patients (“shortening the fever”), and prevention is what the makers disclaimed.
distractors.augment: Trap pair with bolster: true synonyms meaning to strengthen, the wrong direction.
distractors.presage: To foretell; a treatment does not announce a disease.

questions.prompt: The shuttered sickrooms that physicians prescribed to keep out the night air, which they held to carry fever, were themselves ___: patients lay for weeks breathing their own exhalations and the smoke of tallow lamps.

explanation.key: “Themselves” puts the sickrooms alongside the night air they were meant to shut out, and the colon explains how: stale breath and lamp smoke for weeks. The rooms were harmful: deleterious and noxious.

distractors.sterile: Fits the physicians' aim of a clean, sealed room, but the colon describes stale breath and lamp smoke, the opposite of sterile, and it has no partner.
distractors.salutary: Trap pair with salubrious: true synonyms (healthful), the physicians' intention rather than the result.
distractors.opulent: Luxurious; nothing about the rooms' richness.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: refute the interpretation of the 1929 cable breaks that made turbidity currents a favored explanation for features of the deep seafloor
trace how a phenomenon once known only from the laboratory came to be accepted as an agent shaping the deep seafloor
endorse an inference drawn from a historical record while questioning how far that record supports a broader generalization
reconcile the evidence of the 1929 cable breaks with the evidence from the cable breaks off Taiwan in 2006
argue that small turbidity currents, rather than large ones, cut the canyons of the continental margins

explanation.key: C: The second paragraph accepts the 1952 inference (“hard to explain any other way,” later confirmed) but argues that the one measured flow cannot show what is typical, so treating it as archetypal goes too far: it qualifies, not rejects. A uses the wrong verb: the author upholds the interpretation. B covers only the first paragraph. D: the Taiwan breaks confirm the 1929 reading; there is nothing to reconcile. E overclaims: the author says the record cannot decide between rare large flows and many small ones.

questions.prompt: Consider each of the choices separately and select all that apply. The passage suggests which of the following about the record of cable breaks from 1929?
choices: It may overstate the speed at which most of the sediment in the 1929 flow traveled.
It went unexamined for two decades because the repair logs had not noted when each cable failed.
It is consistent with the canyons' having been cut chiefly by flows much smaller than the one it records.

explanation.key: A: Yes. The computed speeds describe the leading edge, “the fastest part” of a flow whose body may have moved far more slowly, so they may overstate how fast most of it moved. B: No. Half right: the record was overlooked, but the logs “had recorded all along” the order and timing of the breaks. C: Yes. A single event “says nothing about whether” the canyons were cut by rare large flows or many smaller ones, so the record leaves the small-flow account open.

questions.prompt: In the context in which it appears, “wanting” most nearly means

explanation.key: B: To be “found wanting” by a standard is to be judged as falling short of it, the sense of “wanting” as lacking. A, D and E take the everyday sense of wanting as desiring or requiring; C (missed) reads it as absent, which does not fit novels judged against a standard.

questions.prompt: Select the sentence in which the author concedes a limit to the passage's defense of the novels' digressions.

explanation.key: The fourth sentence (“None of this makes every digression a success …”) grants that some digressions were padding written under deadline and pay-by-the-sheet pressure, a concession that the journal context does not redeem them all. The second sentence states the critics' charge, not a concession; the last sentence returns to the defense.

questions.prompt: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain the absence of recovery in the eastern valleys without casting doubt on the ecologists' account of the recovery elsewhere?
choices: Elk in the eastern valleys browse the brushy stream banks as heavily as they did before the wolves returned.
Erosion long ago cut the eastern valleys' streams into deep channels, leaving the water table along their banks below the reach of willow roots.
Beavers, whose dams raise the water table along streams, have recolonized the range's western valleys since the wolves were reintroduced.
Elk numbers in the eastern valleys are about the same as in the rest of the range.
In the western valleys, willows have also recovered along stream banks that are open and offer wolves no cover.

explanation.key: B: If willows cannot reach water along the eastern streams, they would fail there whatever the elk do, so the eastern case is explained by something other than browsing and the fear account of the western recovery is untouched. A explains the eastern failure but breaks the constraint: elk ignoring wolves at brushy banks is what the account says should not happen. C offers a rival cause for the recovery elsewhere, undermining the account. D deepens the puzzle rather than explaining it. E shows recovery where the account predicts none, again undermining it.

questions.prompt: For two centuries the parish remembered the ferryman as the drunkard who drowned a wedding party, and no one thought to question the story until the coroner's notes turned up last year among a solicitor's papers. They ___ him more thoroughly than any advocate could have hoped to: the river, they record, had risen four feet in the night, and the ferryman was pulled from it still holding a bridesmaid he had kept afloat for an hour.

explanation.key: The ferryman has been blamed for two centuries, and “more thoroughly than any advocate could have hoped to” casts the notes as his defense. The colon supplies their evidence: a flood, not drink, and a man found saving a passenger. They clear him of blame: exculpate.

distractors.incriminate: The parish story did that; “any advocate” makes the notes a defense, not a charge.
distractors.eulogize: The rescue invites praise, but an advocate answers a charge rather than delivering a eulogy, and the flood detail matters only as an answer to the charge.
distractors.divulge: To reveal information; it takes a secret, not a person, as its object.
distractors.indemnify: To secure against financial loss, not to clear of blame.

questions.prompt: Those who assume that a profession will (i) ___ a principle the moment it becomes costly should consider the engravers' society, which held to its ban on machine-ruled plates through twenty years in which the ban lost its members nearly every banknote contract in the country. It gave up the ban only once the machines had grown so common that refusing them no longer set a hand engraver apart, and even then its members went on insisting that machine work (ii) ___ the craft.

explanation.key: (i) The engravers are offered as a counterexample to the assumption (“should consider”): they kept the ban through twenty costly years. So the assumption is that a profession drops a principle as soon as it costs something: readily jettison. (ii) “Even then” says the members kept the belief behind the ban after giving the ban up, and a ban on machine work rests on the belief that it lowered the craft: debased.

distractors.steadfastly uphold: Turns the assumption into what the engravers actually did, so they would confirm it rather than be a case to “consider” against it.
distractors.quietly codify: Writing a principle down when it becomes costly is no assumption the engravers' story could test.
distractors.dignified: Opposite polarity; no one bans what dignifies the craft.
distractors.safeguarded: Same problem: the ban would be pointless.

questions.prompt: His contemporaries found the court poet's verses (i) ___, so smooth in their vowels that listeners claimed they could be sung without a tune. That smoothness is precisely what earned him (ii) ___ the next generation, who heard in it the sound of a man with nothing to say and every reason to please. Yet drafts found last century, folded into the bindings of books he had given away, show that he (iii) ___ his sharpest lines where no patron would ever read them.

explanation.key: (i) Vowels so smooth the verses could be sung without a tune describe sweetness of sound, and “that smoothness is precisely what earned him” sets up a later reversal of a contemporary verdict: mellifluous. (ii) Hearing “a man with nothing to say and every reason to please” is scorn: the opprobrium of. (iii) “Yet” turns on the charge of emptiness; drafts folded into bindings where no patron would read them were hidden: secreted, in its sense of concealed, not discharged.

distractors.incisive: Sharpness is what the drafts reveal and contemporaries never saw.
distractors.insipid: The next generation's verdict, not his contemporaries'; it would leave no reversal for “precisely.”
distractors.the indulgence of: Tolerance does not fit hearing in him “nothing to say.”
distractors.declaimed: Reciting aloud contradicts placing lines where no one would read them.
distractors.dedicated: Dedications address patrons, the readers he was avoiding.

questions.prompt: The inspectors never troubled to (i) ___ whether the pupils' poor reading owed more to the teaching or to the absence of books in their homes, so their report, though it presents its central finding as (ii) ___, rests on a guess. The (iii) ___ program it recommends may therefore end by drilling children in skills they already have while leaving the real deficiency untouched.

explanation.key: (i) “So … rests on a guess”: they never found out which cause was at work: ascertain. (ii) “Though” contrasts the presentation with the guess, so the report claims certainty: an incontrovertible fact. (iii) A program meant to fix a deficiency, which may miss “the real deficiency”: remedial.

distractors.divulge: Failing to tell others would not make their own finding a guess.
distractors.dispute: Nothing in the sentence was there to dispute; the failure is one of finding out.
distractors.a tentative hypothesis: A guess presented as tentative leaves “though” with no contrast.
distractors.a matter of opinion: Same problem: no contrast with resting on a guess.
distractors.accelerated: A program for faster progress, not for a deficiency.
distractors.extracurricular: Outside the curriculum; says nothing about correcting a deficiency.

questions.prompt: Her colleagues never thought the cataloguer quick, and still less tireless (she kept short hours, took long holidays and set aside any problem that had not yielded within the week), but she was so ___ in her habits of work that the forty years since her death have turned up not one error in the thousands of dates she assigned.

explanation.key: “But” turns from what she lacked (speed, stamina) to what explains her flawless record; “in her habits of work” points to care over detail: meticulous and punctilious.

distractors.indefatigable: Trap pair with dogged: true synonyms for tireless persistence, which “still less tireless” and setting problems aside rule out.
distractors.erudite: Learning could avoid errors, but it is not a habit of work and has no partner here.
distractors.trenchant: Incisive in expression; about style, not accuracy.

questions.prompt: Within a month of the epidemic's end the council voted to ___ the quarantine ordinance, not suspending it for the season as it had in each of the two previous years, but in a form that would oblige any later council wishing to restore it to begin the legislative process anew.

explanation.key: Not a suspension, and done so that restoring the ordinance would mean legislating from scratch: the council revoked it outright. Rescind and annul.

distractors.codify: To set down systematically in law; a council wishing to “restore” the ordinance implies it was removed, not written up.
distractors.curtail: To cut back, not to cancel; there would be nothing to restore.
distractors.ratify: Trap pair with endorse: approval, the wrong direction.

questions.prompt: The more warmly her colleagues praised the pavilion, the more insistently its architect seemed to ___ it, reminding anyone who would listen that its plan was borrowed from a Kyoto teahouse and that its one novelty, the cantilevered roof, had leaked in the first autumn storm.

explanation.key: The proportional frame sets her response against the praise, and the reminders (a borrowed design, a novelty that failed) all lower the pavilion's merit: she belittles and disparages her own work.

distractors.exalt: Trap pair with aggrandize: true synonyms, the colleagues' attitude rather than hers.
distractors.explicate: Pointing out sources is a kind of explanation, but the reminders are chosen to diminish, and nothing pairs with it.
distractors.defend: Praise needs no defense, and recalling a leaking roof does not defend the pavilion.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the organization of the third paragraph?
choices: A view is endorsed without reservation, and evidence is then offered that extends it to a case its proponents had not considered.

A view is partly conceded, an inference its proponents are said to draw from it is rejected, evidence against that inference is offered, and the paragraph closes by assigning a fault that the view had denied.
An inference is rejected, a concession is then made to those who drew it, and evidence is offered suggesting that the concession was premature.
Two accounts of an episode are compared, and the paragraph concludes that each is mistaken in the same respect.
A view is partly conceded, evidence is offered in its support, and the paragraph closes by rejecting the older account altogether.

explanation.key: B: The paragraph concedes the revisionists are right about Lind's theory, rejects their slide to “the result was unavailable,” supports the rejection with the surgeons' journals, and ends by placing the fault with the institution (the scandal the revisionists said was no scandal). A omits the rejection. C reverses the first two moves. D: the older story and the revisionists are not said to err in the same respect. E has the evidence supporting the conceded view and the close rejecting the older story, both the reverse of the paragraph.

questions.prompt: The revisionist historians described in the passage would most likely regard the “scandalous delay” featured in the standard history as
choices: a genuine institutional failure that the standard history attributes to the wrong cause
a misreading that arises from crediting Lind's trial with a significance no one at the time had reason to see in it
evidence that Blane's advocacy was less influential than is usually supposed
a delay that Lind himself regretted and tried to shorten
the result of the navy's reluctance to adopt a remedy whose preparation was costly

explanation.key: B: The revisionists hold that “the delay was not inertia at all” because no one, Lind included, had reason to regard the trial as decisive; the delay looks scandalous only if the trial is read with hindsight. A is the author's own view in the third paragraph, given to the cited party. C reverses their claim that adoption owed more to Blane. D and E are unsupported: Lind did not see the trial as decisive, and cost is never mentioned.

questions.prompt: Consider each of the choices separately and select all that apply. The passage mentions which of the following?
choices: A remedy whose method of preparation undermined its effectiveness
A physician whose advocacy is credited with contributing to the navy's adoption of citrus
Observations by naval surgeons that predate Blane's writing on scurvy

explanation.key: A: Yes. Lind's boiled concentrate of lemon juice, whose preparation “destroyed most of the vitamin it contained” (second paragraph). B: Yes. Gilbert Blane, to whose advocacy the adoption “owed more” than to Lind (second paragraph). C: Yes. Several surgeons recorded that citrus-fed crews stayed well “before Blane had written a word on the subject” (third paragraph).

questions.prompt: Select the sentence that best shows that the author's attitude toward the revisionist account is not wholly critical.

explanation.key: The eighth sentence (“The revisionists are right about Lind's theory, and right that the trial meant less to him than it does to us”) is the author's explicit agreement with part of the account, which, with the objection that follows, makes the stance mixed rather than hostile. The second-paragraph sentences state the revisionist view in its proponents' voice and show nothing of the author's attitude; the ninth through twelfth sentences object to the account or draw the author's own conclusion.

questions.prompt: The passage suggests that the author would most likely agree with which of the following statements about an object correctly classified as a skeuomorph?
choices: Its classification implies that its maker valued the original material more highly than the new one.
Its classification leaves open whether its maker could have afforded an object in the original material.
It should not be so classified until it has been shown whether emulation or habit produced it.
It is more likely to have been made in clay than in metal or stone.
Its copied feature is likely to have been rendered less faithfully over time as the original became rare.

explanation.key: B: The term “merely names a pattern” produced by two processes. Only emulation involves a cheap substitute for an original the maker could not afford; habit (the iron bridges' carpentry joints) has nothing to do with cost. So the label alone leaves affordability open. A gives the emulation view, one of the two processes, as if the term implied it. C reverses the passage: the object is classified by its form, and the process is the open question. D is unsupported; the examples include stone and iron. E reverses the emulation prediction (emulation lapses once the original ceases to be rare).

questions.prompt: Which of the following findings would the author most likely regard as evidence that the molded rivets on a series of clay cups reflect emulation rather than habit?
choices: The rivets on the cups grow steadily shallower over several centuries, at much the same rate in every workshop.
Cups with rivets are found in the same graves as bronze cups, often placed beside them.
The rivets are rendered most exactly on cups from the period when bronze cups were scarcest and disappear soon after bronze becomes common.
The rivets on the cups occupy the same positions that rivets occupied on the bronze cups.
The potters who made the cups also made other vessels that imitated wooden forms.

explanation.key: C: The author's test is that emulation is “most faithful where the original was most admired” and lapses “once the original ceases to be rare”; fidelity tracking bronze's scarcity is that signature. A is the signature of habit (slow erosion regardless of the model). B shares the topic of prestige but not the author's criterion, and owners of bronze cups had no need of a cheap substitute. D shows only that the cups copy bronze, which both processes predict. E is irrelevant to which process kept the rivets.

questions.prompt: The passage provides information to answer which of the following questions?
choices: Which English translator was the first to render Hafez's ghazals?
Why did the compilers of manuscript anthologies reorder the couplets of ghazals?
What were some of the stock images on which ghazal poets drew?
When did Persian commentators begin ranking ghazals by the links between their couplets?
How many couplets did a ghazal ordinarily contain?

explanation.key: C: The passage names the moth and the candle and the nightingale and the rose as stock images. A: The translator is neither named nor said to be the first. B: The passage offers two rival readings of the reordering and settles neither. D: No date is given for the commentators' practice. E: Only that each couplet stood complete, not how many there were.

questions.prompt: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the officials' conclusion?
choices: The menus, portion sizes and length of the lunch period at the district's elementary schools were the same in both years.
In a neighboring district that kept recess after lunch, food waste fell by a similar amount over the same year.
Teachers in the Ashby district reported that students were calmer in afternoon classes after the change.
Most of the food thrown away in both years consisted of vegetables and fruit.

explanation.key: A: Rules out the obvious rival causes of less waste (food children liked better, smaller portions, more time to eat), leaving the schedule change as the likely cause. B weakens: waste fell just as much without the change. C concerns behavior in class, not eating. D and E are true in both years and bear on neither the change nor its cause.
